PAS: Changes Partners Like Changing Clothes — Now Dumps BERSATU for UMNO Lifeline 

PAS is desperately begging UMNO for a political lifeline.

The photo above says it all. 

While UMNO holds its Biro Politik meeting at Hotel Seri Pacific, PAS bigwigs — including Takiyuddin and Naib President Ustaz Idris Ahmad — are already lurking in the same hotel. 

This is not coincidence. This is desperation in action.

PAS knows the hard truth: there is no Green Wave in Johor.

Bangsa Johor has consistently rejected PAS’s brand of extremism, racial politics, and religious authoritarianism. 

Johoreans do not want outsiders dictating what they can eat, wear, or how they should live their lives. 

They reject the constant haram-halal policing and the radical tone that comes with it.

Look at the last Johor state election.

Even at the height of the so-called Green Wave in the northern states, PAS only managed to win one single state seat  in Johor — Maharani — and that too with an embarrassingly slim majority. 

In the parliamentary seats? Zero. A complete shutout.

Now, sensing total annihilation in the upcoming Johor election, PAS is rushing to resell Muafakat Nasional 2.0. 

The narrative was first floated by Annuar Musa, then amplified by Tuan Ibrahim and PAS Youth. Classic desperation move.

This is not a “grand alliance” based on principle. 

They change partners like changing clothes. 

Last GE, they cozied up to Bersatu. Why? Election funding. 

Bersatu had the war chest, so PAS became their best friend.

Now Bersatu’s bank accounts are frozen and their political value has tanked. 

Suddenly, PAS is already at UMNO’s hotel door, hawking Muafakat Nasional 2.0.

They’re still technically with Perikatan Nasional, but already shopping for a new partner. 

This is betrayal in progress.

Bersatu hasn’t even been buried yet and PAS is already at the wake eyeing UMNO.

PAS will stab anybody to gain power. They blew with Bersatu when the money was flowing. Now the wind is shifting toward UMNO, so they’re blowing that way. No principle, no ideology — just raw opportunism.

This is a failing party crawling on its knees, begging UMNO to throw them a lifeline so they don’t get wiped out entirely in the south. Without some form of seat arrangement or pact, PAS faces political extinction in Johor.

The beggar has arrived at the palace gate.

Johor has always been moderate, pragmatic, and development-focused. The people here value stability and progress over performative religiosity and divisive politics. 

PAS knows this — which is why they are panicking and trying to force their way back into relevance through the backdoor.

The message to PAS is simple:

Johor doesn’t want you. 

No amount of hotel lobbying and desperate begging will change that.

PAS: The Ultimate Political Frog

2015: Dumps Pakatan Rakyat to form Gagasan Sejahtera with Ikatan. Blames DAP.

2020: Dumps Gagasan, jumps to Muafakat Nasional with UMNO. Calls it “Ummah unity”.

2020: Joins Perikatan Nasional with Bersatu too. Double dipping.

2022: GE15 with Bersatu because they had election funds. Wins big in the north.

2024-2026: Bersatu accounts frozen, leaders charged. PAS now lurking at UMNO meetings selling Muafakat 2.0.

They go wherever the power and money go. Today Bersatu, tomorrow UMNO, next week whoever.

 No loyalty. No principle. Just survival.

Muafakat Nasional Set to Storm Back: BN-PAS Alliance Poised for 116-Seat Majority

The Muafakat Nasional alliance between Barisan Nasional (BN) and PAS could form the next federal government with a majority of 116 seats in Parliament. 

This projection is based on expected vote swings in marginal seats currently held by Pakatan Harapan (PH) and Bersatu (PN), where many Malay voters may shift support to UMNO or PAS.

Basis of the Projection and Calculation Method

This data and seat-by-seat calculation is derived from the results of the (GE15) in 2022, assuming a straight 1-on-1 contest under a revived Muafakat Nasional alliance (no three-cornered fights between UMNO/BN and PAS).

Example: Lembah Pantai (currently held by Fahmi Fadzil of PKR)

In GE15: Fahmi Fadzil (PH-PKR) won with 35,359 votes.

UMNO (BN) came second with 21,447 votes.
PAS (PN) came third with 19,098 votes.

In a Muafakat Nasional 1-on-1 scenario: PAS’s 19,098 votes would transfer/add to UMNO’s candidate, giving UMNO a combined 40,545 votes – beating PKR’s 35,359 by a majority of 5,186 votes. 

Thus, Lembah Pantai swings to UMNO.

For the rest of the seats listed, you can apply the same formula:

Identify the GE15 votes for PH/Bersatu winner vs. UMNO/BN and PAS/PN candidates.

Combine UMNO + PAS votes and compare to the winner’s tally.

Account for potential Malay voter consolidation and Bersatu seats (many won on PAS grassroots support in PN).

Seats currently held by Bersatu are particularly vulnerable, as much of their support came from PAS voters and machinery under the Perikatan Nasional banner.

Why Muafakat Nasional is a Deadly Combination:

UMNO provides strong leadership, institutional experience, and resources.

PAS supplies powerful grassroots networks, election machinery, and a loyal voter base.

This alliance stands strong on Peninsular Malaysia alone and does not rely on any pacts with Borneo-based parties (GPS, GRS, etc.) to form the federal government.

PAS: Currently 43 seats → Gains at least 9 more → 52 seats

UMNO: Currently 26 seats (after deducting 7 Sabah seats, assuming total loss, leaving 19) → Adds 33 new seats → 55 seats

MCA: Currently 2 seats → Adds 5 → 7 seats

MIC: Currently 1 seat → Adds 1 → 2 seats

Total for BN + PAS (Muafakat Nasional): 116 seats – sufficient for a simple majority (112 out of 222 parliamentary seats).

Meanwhile, PH and Bersatu face significant losses:

PETALING JAYA: An Amanah leader has told Negeri Sembilan Barisan Nasional to reconsider its intention to form a new state government with Perikatan Nasional after withdrawing support for menteri besar Aminuddin Harun.

Amanah central committee member Sany Hamzan said BN should look back on its past experience working with PN before deciding to form an alliance in Negeri Sembilan.

He told FMT that PN merely wanted to take advantage of the ongoing turmoil and take part in a new state government.

“Umno and BN need to remember their experience working with PN before this,” he said, pointing to the time when PN and BN were allies in the federal government from 2020 to 2022.

PN and BN joined hands to form the federal government, with Bersatu president Muhyiddin Yassin becoming the prime minister, following the collapse of the Pakatan Harapan administration in February 2020.

Muhyiddin resigned as the prime minister in August 2021 after several BN MPs withdrew support for him, and Umno vice-president Ismail Sabri Yaakob replaced him in the top post.

Despite being allies, Umno and PN were frequently at each other’s throats and eventually clashed in the Melaka and Johor state elections despite being federal allies.

Umno has consistently accused PAS of betraying their Muafakat Nasional pact by co-founding PN with Bersatu.

Sany, the Amanah election director, said PH had been magnanimous towards BN in Selangor, intentionally making room for Umno to join the state executive council while allocating local councillor and village chief posts.

The Hulu Langat MP said issues within a state administration should be dealt with through negotiations rather than withdrawing support or resigning from posts.

Since the Negeri Sembilan government was formed on the basis of the PH-BN unity pact, Sany said, all parties should go back to the negotiation table to sort out their dispute.

He said the crisis in Negeri Sembilan was not just political but involved the state’s royal and customary institutions.

The Negeri Sembilan crisis arose after Mubarak Dohak, the former undang of Sungai Ujong, announced the removal of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang di-Pertuan Besar with the three other undangs on April 19.

However, Aminuddin said the state government did not recognise Tuanku Muhriz’s removal, as Mubarak had been lawfully removed as undang on May 13 last year for contravening 33 customary laws.

Following that, all 14 Umno assemblymen announced that they had withdrawn support for Aminuddin as the menteri besar, saying it was linked to the crisis involving the chieftains and Tuanku Muhriz.

Negeri Sembilan BN later claimed it had a simple majority in the 36-seat assembly to form the state government, with the support of PN’s five assemblymen.

However, Aminuddin said Tuanku Muhriz wanted him to continue as the menteri besar until the question of his majority support was determined.

Akmal Saleh’s Big Lie Exposed: UMNO Lost Malays Long Before DAP – Thanks to Your Own Corruption & Arrogance

Akmal Saleh, listen up and listen hard—you're peddling a load of half-baked lies that stink of desperation. 

It's not DAP that's costing UMNO Malay support; it's your party's own rotten history of corruption, blatant racism, and insufferable arrogance that's driven you straight into the gutter. 

At your precious Pemuda UMNO convention, you paraded "facts" claiming UMNO lost Malay votes after teaming up with DAP. 

What a joke—that's not the truth; that's a pathetic half-truth designed to dodge accountability.

Let's slap some real numbers in your face.

UMNO once commanded a whopping 75% Malay support. 

In GE14—without a whiff of DAP—your support cratered to 45%. 

Then GE15 rolls around, still no DAP in sight, and it plunges further to 35%. 

Now, after partnering with DAP, you're whining about 27%? 

That's a measly 8% drop. 

But wake up, Akmal: Before DAP ever entered the picture, you'd already hemorrhaged a massive 40% from 75% to 35%. 

That's your own self-inflicted disaster, not DAP's fault. 

And that 55% of your core UMNO supporters who bolted to PN in GE15? 

They didn't flock to DAP—they ditched you for your rivals. DAP gained zilch from your implosion.

Now you're bleating about losing rural support? 

Spare us the crocodile tears. 

Is this your way of admitting Zahid Hamidi is a total failure as Menteri Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah? 

Rural development and kampung welfare fall squarely on his shoulders, not a single DAP minister's. 

Those rural seats didn't go to DAP—they were snatched by PAS and Bersatu. 

And here's the killer question, Akmal: Do you seriously think cozying up to PAS now will let UMNO claw back those seats? 

Hell no—the incumbents will cling to them like glue. 

It's only through the Madani coalition—with DAP in it—that UMNO has any shot at reclaiming them from PAS and Bersatu. 

Proof? 

Post-GE15, with DAP on board, you crushed the by-elections in Pelangai, Mahkota, Ayer Kuning, and Nenggiri with overwhelming majorities. 

Shoving the blame for your epic failures onto DAP isn't just irresponsible—it's gutless and utterly illogical.

Let's not forget who the real backstabbers are. 

It was PAS that betrayed UMNO, ditching Muafakat Nasional to slither into PN with Bersatu. Not DAP. 

For 33 months under PN, PAS propped up that regime while they poached your members, schemed to dissolve UMNO, froze your party accounts, and dragged your leaders through the courts like criminals. Not DAP. 

But under Madani—with DAP in the mix—Zahid got his DNAA, Rosmah walked free, and cases against Tok Mat and LCS were buried, all investigations that festered under PN's watch. 

Funny how that works, huh?

Then you have the audacity to demand a MN revival so "Malay states" like Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu can "develop," claiming development's only pouring into Johor, Penang, and Klang Valley. 

What a brazen distortion. 

DAP's been in power for barely three years—it's UMNO and PN's Malay-led governments that squandered nearly 70 years failing to lift those states out of poverty. 

Under Madani, the annual budgets for Kelantan, Kedah, and Terengganu dwarf what's given to Penang. 

And why do Penang, Johor, KL, and Selangor thrive? 

Not because of some magical government handout—it's the progressive, driven societies there fueling their own economies. 

Forced, artificial "development" flops like Forest City every time. 

So own it, Akmal: It's Malay leadership and society that's let those states rot, not DAP.

Crunch these numbers, since you love "facts".

There are 5,229,000 Malays in the SG4 states (Kedah: 1,803,000; Kelantan: 1,935,000; Terengganu: 1,236,000; Perlis: 255,000).

But dwarfing that? 

9,722,000 Malays in Selangor (4,153,000), Perak (1,530,000), Negeri Sembilan (761,000), Pulau Pinang (736,000), and Johor (2,542,000). 

Federal allocations to Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu already outstrip the rest—no issue there. 

But the second aid trickles to Penang, your walaun PN cronies erupt in outrage, even though Penang pumps among the highest GDP and revenue into the nation while getting the skimpiest allocations. 

Why the selective rage? 

Why act like there are no Malays in Penang? Those 736,000 Malays aren't real? No PAS members, supporters, or voters there? Only SG4 Malays count as "pure"?

This is peak hypocrisy from you walaun types.

You abandon your hometowns, dump your parents and grandparents in backwardness, and flock to developed states like KL, Selangor, Johor, and Penang to chase jobs and prosperity. 

Every five years, you crawl back to vote in PAS administrations that perpetuate poverty and underdevelopment in your birth states, then return to leech off the progress in non-PAS territories.

And when aid flows to those thriving states—where you live, work, and eat—you screech like hypocrites, pretending you don't benefit. What kind of twisted logic is this? 

You smear these places as capitalist dens of liberalism, vice, entertainment, and un-Islamic filth, accuse the ruling parties of every sin under the sun—yet you happily soak up their advancements and amenities. 

You vote PAS back home to keep it poor and regressive, while refusing to live there yourself. 

Demanding handouts for states you won't even stay in?

Pathetic. 

Grow a spine, Akmal—face your party's mess instead of scapegoating DAP. Your downfall is all on you.

PETALING JAYA: Johor Umno Youth has urged PAS to embrace the Rumah Bangsa initiative as a platform for uniting Malays, in response to the Islamic party’s proposal that efforts to unite Malay-based political parties should begin in Johor ahead of the upcoming state election.

Its chief, Noor Azleen Ambros, told FMT that Johor Umno Youth welcomed PAS’s intention and aspiration to foster Malay unity, but hoped the effort would be carried out sincerely and not merely as an electoral strategy.

He said PAS’s decision on whether to contest independently or cooperate with others in the Johor state election would serve as a litmus test of the Islamic party’s sincerity.

“The choice is entirely up to PAS,” he told FMT.

Yesterday, PAS deputy president Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man called on PAS and Umno to work together in the Johor state election, describing it as the right time to revive their now-defunct Muafakat Nasional alliance.

Tuan Ibrahim said cooperation between the country’s two largest Malay-Muslim parties was needed and that the state polls could usher in a new political realignment.

“In that regard, Johor Umno Youth’s suggestion is for PAS to consider Rumah Bangsa as a platform to pursue that goal,” Noor Azleen said.

Meanwhile, Umno Supreme Council member Nur Jazlan Mohamed claimed PAS was raising the issue of Malay unity only at a time when Perikatan Nasional was in a weakened position.

According to him, the issue of MN was never seriously discussed when PN was in power.

“Now that they are in the opposition and weakened, with PN fractured and facing a shortage of resources ahead of the next election, they have suddenly begun talking about Malay unity,” he said.

The senator also took aim at what he described as PAS’s long-standing political approach of “using Islam as a tool to divide the Malays”.

The Johor state assembly was dissolved on Monday, paving the way for the 16th Johor state election, which must be held within 60 days.

BN, PH and PN have each said they will be contesting all 56 seats.

The Future of Perikatan Nasional: From Bersatu's Turmoil to PAS's Ascendancy and Electoral Prospects
By Betty Teh 

Perikatan Nasional (PN), Malaysia's primary opposition coalition, finds itself at a pivotal crossroads as the nation inches toward the 16th General Election (GE16), due possibly by mid 2027. Formed in 2020 amid political upheaval, PN comprising Parti Pribumi Bersatu Malaysia (Bersatu), Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS), Gerakan, and the Malaysian Indian People’s Party (MIPP) has been a formidable force, capitalising on Malay Muslim support to secure 74 seats in the 2022 general election (GE15). 

However, recent internal fractures, particularly within Bersatu, have exposed vulnerabilities that could reshape the coalition's trajectory. This analysis begins with the latest developments in Bersatu, explores PAS's growing dominance, assesses Bersatu's potential fate, and concludes with a forecast for PN's performance in the upcoming polls.

Recent Happenings in Bersatu: A Leadership Exodus and Brewing Crisis

Bersatu, once the linchpin of PN under the stewardship of former Prime Minister Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin, has been plagued by internal discord that culminated in a dramatic series of resignations at the end of 2025. On December 30, 2025, Muhyiddin announced his resignation as PN chairman, effective January 1, 2026, citing unresolved tensions within the coalition. 

This move triggered a cascade of departures from key Bersatu figures, including Datuk Seri Mohamed Azmin Ali, who stepped down as PN secretary-general and Selangor PN chairman; Datuk Dr Sahruddin Jamal as Johor PN chairman; Datuk Seri Ahmad Faizal Azumu as Perak PN chairman; and Mohamad Hanifah Abu Baker as Negeri Sembilan PN chairman.

These resignations stem from longstanding frictions, including a public feud over leadership succession and strategic direction. Throughout 2025, Bersatu grappled with calls for Muhyiddin, now 78, to relinquish his role as party president and PN's prime ministerial candidate. Internal rifts were exacerbated by defections of six Bersatu MPs pledged support to Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's unity government without formally leaving the party, weakening Bersatu's parliamentary presence from 24 to an effective lower count. 

By November 2025, the party's Supreme Council committed to resolving these issues harmoniously, prioritizing unity ahead of state elections like Sabah's. However, the December exodus has been described as PN's most severe crisis since its inception, highlighting a "crack waiting to split" amid power struggles.

Bersatu's financial contributions during GE15, including funding PAS's campaigns that led to its record 43 seats, have also resurfaced as a point of contention, with former aides accusing PAS of ingratitude. Despite the turmoil, Bersatu has reaffirmed its commitment to PN, with leaders urging Muhyiddin to reconsider his resignation and pledging adherence to coalition consensus.

PAS's Dominance in PN: From Coalition Partner to De Facto Leader

PAS's rise within PN has been unmistakable, fueled by its electoral strength and ideological appeal. Holding 43 of PN's 67 parliamentary seats, PAS is the coalition's largest component, dwarfing Bersatu's diminished influence. The "Green Wave" of GE15 and subsequent state polls in 2023 propelled PAS to control four states: Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah, and Perlis; cementing its narrative dominance on Islam and Malay Muslim issues.

The recent Bersatu resignations have accelerated PAS's ascendancy. PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang announced on January 2, 2026, that the party will assume PN's chairmanship, with a candidate to be named soon. Analysts note that PAS's stability contrasts sharply with Bersatu's chaos, positioning it as the "only strong party" in PN. Tensions, such as the Perlis state crisis where PAS and Bersatu clashed over governance, underscore a broader power struggle for dominance ahead of GE16.

PAS's ideological purism emphasizing Islamic governance without compromise gives it a narrative edge, allowing experimentation with cultural assets to appeal to conservative voters. However, this dominance raises concerns: a PAS led PN could alienate non Malay voters, limiting the coalition's urban appeal. Some speculate this could revive old pacts like Muafakat Nasional with UMNO, though obstacles persist.

One must remember PAS does not need PN to survive.

What Will Happen to Bersatu? A Strategic Retreat or Irrelevance?

Bersatu's future within PN appears tied to a "strategic step back" rather than outright dissolution. Muhyiddin, retaining his presidency, emphasized on January 2, 2026, that Bersatu remains a "principled, consistent, and loyal partner" in PN, prioritizing party survival and unity. This retreat aims to reorganize leadership and fortify internal structures amid challenges like defections and financial strains.

Yet, risks abound. If Bersatu exits PN entirely a scenario floated amid the crisis it could contest independently, targeting former UMNO strongholds now under PN. Analysts warn this might fragment the opposition vote, benefiting Anwar's Pakatan Harapan (PH)-led government. Bersatu's survival hinges on attracting disillusioned Malay voters, but without PN's umbrella, it risks marginalization, especially as PAS emerges unchallenged. Party insiders stress resolving internal differences, as seen in efforts by figures like Tun Faisal Ismail Aziz.

In essence, Bersatu may endure as a junior partner, focusing on rebuilding for state polls in Melaka (by Feb 2027), Sarawak (by Apr 2027), and Johor (by Jun 2027), but its influence wanes as PAS consolidates power.

Bersatu is not in a position to fight internally or externally. Worst case scenario Bersatu may fade into irrelevance.

Forecasting PN's Performance in GE16: Challenges and Opportunities

PN's prospects in GE16 are clouded by internal divisions and demographic hurdles. Currently holding 67 seats, the coalition must unify before impending state elections, which could serve as bellwethers. The Sabah state polls in late 2025 highlighted PN's struggles: Bersatu won zero seats, while PAS secured its first in the region, but overall, the coalition faltered against PH's multi-ethnic appeal.

Key challenges include PAS's poor perception among non Malays, restricting PN to Malay majority seats and limiting urban gains. Insiders warn that without broadening support, PN's path to Putrajaya is "steeper." Youth voters, who swung toward PN in GE15 (37% under 30s), remain crucial, demanding clear leadership and policies on representation.

Optimistically, a PAS led PN could galvanise conservative bases, potentially expanding in Malay heartlands if Bersatu stabilizes. 

However, self inflicted crises like the leadership vacuum could erode credibility. With Anwar's government stable and focused on economic growth until GE16, PN's fragmentation might hand PH an advantage. Forecasts suggest PN could retain 60-70 seats if unified, but drop below 50 if divisions persist, paving the way for a stronger PH-BN alliance.

PN’s future is possibly an opposition permanently. It is unlikely PN will ever form a federal government. 

In summary, PN's future hinges on navigating Bersatu's retreat and PAS's dominance without alienating broader voters. While resilient in its core base, the coalition risks becoming a PAS-centric entity, potentially limiting its national ambitions in GE16.

It's not DAP that's costing UMNO Malay support; it's your party's own rotten history of corruption, blatant racism, and insufferable arrogance that's driven you straight into the gutter.

Let's slap some real numbers in your face.

UMNO once commanded a whopping 75% Malay support. 

In GE14—without a whiff of DAP—your support cratered to 45%. 

Then GE15 rolls around, still no DAP in sight, and it plunges further to 35%. 

Now, after partnering with DAP, you're whining about 27%? 

That's a measly 8% drop. 

But wake up, Akmal: Before DAP ever entered the picture, you'd already hemorrhaged a massive 40% from 75% to 35%. 

That's your own self-inflicted disaster, not DAP's fault. 

And that 55% of your core UMNO supporters who bolted to PN in GE15? 

They didn't flock to DAP—they ditched you for your rivals. DAP gained zilch from your implosion.

Now you're bleating about losing rural support? 

Spare us the crocodile tears. 

Is this your way of admitting Zahid Hamidi is a total failure as Menteri Kemajuan Desa dan Wilayah? 

Rural development and kampung welfare fall squarely on his shoulders, not a single DAP minister's. 

Those rural seats didn't go to DAP—they were snatched by PAS and Bersatu. 

And here's the killer question, Akmal: Do you seriously think cozying up to PAS now will let UMNO claw back those seats? 

Hell no—the incumbents will cling to them like glue. 

It's only through the Madani coalition—with DAP in it—that UMNO has any shot at reclaiming them from PAS and Bersatu. 

Proof? 

Post-GE15, with DAP on board, you crushed the by-elections in Pelangai, Mahkota, Ayer Kuning, and Nenggiri with overwhelming majorities. 

Shoving the blame for your epic failures onto DAP isn't just irresponsible—it's gutless and utterly illogical.

Let's not forget who the real backstabbers are. 

It was PAS that betrayed UMNO, ditching Muafakat Nasional to slither into PN with Bersatu. Not DAP. 

For 33 months under PN, PAS propped up that regime while they poached your members, schemed to dissolve UMNO, froze your party accounts, and dragged your leaders through the courts like criminals. Not DAP. 

But under Madani—with DAP in the mix—Zahid got his DNAA, Rosmah walked free, and cases against Tok Mat and LCS were buried, all investigations that festered under PN's watch. 

Funny how that works, huh?

Then you have the audacity to demand a MN revival so "Malay states" like Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu can "develop," claiming development's only pouring into Johor, Penang, and Klang Valley. 

What a brazen distortion. 

DAP's been in power for barely three years—it's UMNO and PN's Malay-led governments that squandered nearly 70 years failing to lift those states out of poverty. 

Under Madani, the annual budgets for Kelantan, Kedah, and Terengganu dwarf what's given to Penang. 

And why do Penang, Johor, KL, and Selangor thrive? 

Not because of some magical government handout—it's the progressive, driven societies there fueling their own economies. 

Forced, artificial "development" flops like Forest City every time. 

So own it, Akmal: It's Malay leadership and society that's let those states rot, not DAP.

Crunch these numbers, since you love "facts".

There are 5,229,000 Malays in the SG4 states (Kedah: 1,803,000; Kelantan: 1,935,000; Terengganu: 1,236,000; Perlis: 255,000).

But dwarfing that? 

9,722,000 Malays in Selangor (4,153,000), Perak (1,530,000), Negeri Sembilan (761,000), Pulau Pinang (736,000), and Johor (2,542,000). 

Federal allocations to Kedah, Kelantan, and Terengganu already outstrip the rest—no issue there. 

But the second aid trickles to Penang, your walaun PN cronies erupt in outrage, even though Penang pumps among the highest GDP and revenue into the nation while getting the skimpiest allocations. 

Why the selective rage? 

Why act like there are no Malays in Penang? Those 736,000 Malays aren't real? No PAS members, supporters, or voters there? Only SG4 Malays count as "pure"?

This is peak hypocrisy from you walaun types.

You abandon your hometowns, dump your parents and grandparents in backwardness, and flock to developed states like KL, Selangor, Johor, and Penang to chase jobs and prosperity. 

Every five years, you crawl back to vote in PAS administrations that perpetuate poverty and underdevelopment in your birth states, then return to leech off the progress in non-PAS territories.

And when aid flows to those thriving states—where you live, work, and eat—you screech like hypocrites, pretending you don't benefit. What kind of twisted logic is this? 

You smear these places as capitalist dens of liberalism, vice, entertainment, and un-Islamic filth, accuse the ruling parties of every sin under the sun—yet you happily soak up their advancements and amenities. 

You vote PAS back home to keep it poor and regressive, while refusing to live there yourself. 

Demanding handouts for states you won't even stay in?

Pathetic. 

Grow a spine, Akmal—face your party's mess instead of scapegoating DAP. Your downfall is all on you.

At the end of this week, Perlis has a new Menteri Besar (chief minister). The PAS Perlis Menteri Besar Mohd Shukri Ramli was disposed and replaced by a new Bersatu Menteri Besar Abu Bakar Hamzah. This occurred after three PAS assembly men Saad Seman of Chuping, Fakhrul Anwar Ismail of Bintong and Ridzuan Hashim of Guar Sanji turned against their leader and toppled Mohd Shukri Ramil (who incidentally has family connections through marriage to the top of the PAS leadership).

On December 30, 2025, Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin announced his resignation as PN chairman, effective January 1, 2026, citing the need for fresh leadership amid ongoing internal tensions. This was quickly followed by a cascade of exits: Mohamed Azmin Ali stepped down as PN secretary-general and Selangor PN liaison chairman; Ahmad Faizal Azumu resigned as Perak PN chairman; Sahruddin Jamal quit as Johor PN chairman; and Mohamad Hanifah Abu Baker withdrew as Negeri Sembilan PN chairman.

A resumption of the Muafakat Nasional (MN) alliance between Bersatu and UMNO and how together they could take government is on top of the list. Some want to believe that PN under a PAS leadership will become more conservative, forcing the “unity government’ under prime minister Anwar Ibrahim to follow suit and also become more conservative and stall needed reforms the government needs to maintain non-Malay support in the next general election. Prime minister Anwar Ibrahim was very quick to point out there are no betrayals or sabotage in the ‘unity government’. This hints of some anxiety, where both DAP and UMNO are involved in deep introspection about their future positions in the Madani government. Yesterday’s resignations were not the move. The resignations were more like shadow boxing, with any move yet to come.

PETALING JAYA: Johor Umno Youth has urged PAS to embrace the Rumah Bangsa initiative as a platform for uniting Malays, in response to the Islamic party’s proposal that efforts to unite Malay-based political parties should begin in Johor ahead of the upcoming state election.

Its chief, Noor Azleen Ambros, told FMT that Johor Umno Youth welcomed PAS’s intention and aspiration to foster Malay unity, but hoped the effort would be carried out sincerely and not merely as an electoral strategy.

He said PAS’s decision on whether to contest independently or cooperate with others in the Johor state election would serve as a litmus test of the Islamic party’s sincerity.

“The choice is entirely up to PAS,” he told FMT.

Yesterday, PAS deputy president Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man called on PAS and Umno to work together in the Johor state election, describing it as the right time to revive their now-defunct Muafakat Nasional alliance.

Tuan Ibrahim said cooperation between the country’s two largest Malay-Muslim parties was needed and that the state polls could usher in a new political realignment.

“In that regard, Johor Umno Youth’s suggestion is for PAS to consider Rumah Bangsa as a platform to pursue that goal,” Noor Azleen said.

An Umno initiative, Rumah Bangsa provided an open platform for anyone wishing to return to or join the party, whether individually or as part of a group.

PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang previously said his party was not prepared to support the initiative to unite the Malays as it is not centred on Islam.

Meanwhile, Umno Supreme Council member Nur Jazlan Mohamed claimed PAS was raising the issue of Malay unity only at a time when Perikatan Nasional was in a weakened position.

According to him, the issue of MN was never seriously discussed when PN was in power.

“Now that they are in the opposition and weakened, with PN fractured and facing a shortage of resources ahead of the next election, they have suddenly begun talking about Malay unity,” he said.

The senator also took aim at what he described as PAS’s long-standing political approach of “using Islam as a tool to divide the Malays”.

The Johor state assembly was dissolved on Monday, paving the way for the 16th Johor state election, which must be held within 60 days.

Barisan Nasional, Pakatan Harapan and PN have said they will be contesting all 56 seats.

Malay unity call falls flat
By Joceline Tan 

THEY are big names in the Malay political world and they are urging the Malays and Muslims to come together under one big umbrella.

There they were - the one and only Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad, Bersatu president Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin and his deputy Datuk Seri Hamzah Zainudin and PAS deputy president Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man.

Two former prime ministers, one aspiring prime minister and the future president of PAS and yet their call for Malay unity has come across like a balloon running out of air.

“I’m sure I was not the only one letting out a long groan and telling myself, oh no, not again. I am not being negative but this seemed to be coming out of nowhere. It all seems a little desperate.

“Sure, there are issues that many out there are unhappy about but I don’t see a singular burning issue galvanising the Malays,” said political risk analyst Datuk Wan Shihab Wan Ismail.

A Kelantan-born professional put it more bluntly: “There has been no traction at all”.

Race dynamics is not new to those in the corridor of power but this Malay unity song and dance is getting a little tiresome.

For a start, those making the call have been around for decades during which they beat the unity drum when it suited them.

The irony is that some of the above personalities used to be arch enemies who accused each other of dividing the Malays, labelled each other as “infidels” and “deviants” and even refused to pray in the same surau.

Wan Shihab said the problem with these personalities is that they are tired faces who sound like voices of yesteryears.

The Malay ground is rumbling but not to the point that they feel that the sky is falling.

Dr Mahathir will be 100 next month, Muhyiddin turned 78 last month while Hamzah is 68 in a field surrounded by young political ambitions. As for Tuan Ibrahim, his imminent ascent in PAS is not drawing much excitement.

Dr Mahathir is such a paradox and it is quite tragic that the toxic politics between him and Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim continues to impact politics today.

“This latest move is about Perikatan Nasional roping in Mahathir as their mascot but he is a spent bullet. People want to take selfies with him but they don’t want him back in the driver’s seat,” said Wan Shihab.

The supreme irony is that the last time that Malays felt they were truly under siege was when Dr Mahathir was prime minister for a second time and presided over what was perceived as a government dominated by non-Malays.

The formation of Muafakat Nasional shook the Mahathir 2.0 government to the core when it took to the streets to oppose the ratification of Icerd or the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination.

“Malay unity has always been a Mahathir playbook. It is still a viable concept but it comes and goes. It becomes louder if the government is perceived as not Malay enough. The market is there although there is no groundswell at this point because Umno is in the government,” said lawyer and political commentator Khaw Veon Szu.

Dr Mahathir’s latest Malay umbrella grouping has closed its doors to Umno but welcomes individual Umno members.

Surely the group knows that Umno wants nothing to do with Dr Mahathir?

Umno has not forgiven Dr Mahathir for bringing down the party, poaching its elected representatives and using the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission to go after its top leadership.

And as Umno Youth leader Datuk Dr Muhamad Akmal Saleh pointed out: “These are the same people who tried to deregister Umno when they were in power. We have not forgotten what happened”.

Umno leaders are not impressed that the man who took down a Malay-dominated government is now preaching about Malay unity.

PAS and Umno are the two formidable Malay political forces. One commands the religious high ground, the other is seen as commanding the moderate Malay ground.

Umno is at its most stable since 2018. It has found its centre of gravity amid the ups and down of the unity government.

As Johor politician Tan Sri Shahrir Samad pointed out, Umno ministers are doing better than their fellow Cabinet members from other parties because they are trained and shaped through a grassroots leadership development process.

“Umno has to be part of the equation. Without Umno, there will be no Malay unity,” said a political insider.

It explains how Umno has become quite central to the survival of the Madani government. Umno represents the Malay stake in the government and it is also able to check the advance of PAS.

The Malay voice, said Khaw, is more complicated than ever because of the contrasting forces of Islamisation, globalisation and modernisation.

The Mahathir umbrella group has vouched to safeguard the future of the community. Unfortunately, its main component PAS has yet to convince people that it is capable of taking the country forward.

“The goal of this Malay unity group is basically about power and forming the government. Malay parties will do well in the next general election but there has to be new blood.

“But politics does not happen in a void, this is a multi-racial society and they will be unable to get very far without addressing non-Malay interests and concerns,” said the above political insider.

The quest for Malay unity is like the holy grail, much desired but somehow beyond reach.

It is also an old song being sung by yesterday’s singers that is unlikely to fade away. But it might have greater traction if it is sung by younger people who represent the future.

当下的国家政治动态再次证明了一个根本事实：当选举风暴逼近时，组织的成熟度与长期的稳定记录才是最有价值的政治筹码。在充满解散州议会传言和东拼西凑政治联盟的乱象中，国民阵线（国阵）继续展现出井然有序的备战状态，成为国家未来稳定的基石。

随着即将敲响的第16届柔佛州选举（PRN）战鼓，公众的焦点已完全转向：哪个政治联盟能够提供真正的实质治理，而非空洞的修辞承诺。

1. 土团党阵营裂痕加剧，国阵地位稳如磐石

土团党柔佛州妇女组（Srikandi）主席兼恩道（Endau）区州议员阿尔威雅（YB Alwiyah Talib）宣布退党并重返巫统的决定，释放了一个明确的信号：反对党阵营正面临严重的信心危机。

相比之下，在拿督斯里阿末扎希领导下的国阵，正以高度纪律和条理分明的方式稳步前进：

系统化筹备： 柔佛全部56个州议席的候选人名单已进入最后的审核与敲定阶段。
 以民为本： 国阵推举的候选人绝非滥竽充数，而是能够确保柔佛持续发展与繁荣的务实人物。
 内部团结坚不可摧： 近期网络上流传一份涉及15名马华候选人的假名单（甚至包括针对拿督斯里魏家祥的抹黑），这恰恰暴露了对手企图离间国阵成员党的绝望手段。国阵绝不会轻易中计，联盟内部的凝聚力极其稳固，绝非廉价网军（Cybertrooper）的伎俩所能动摇。

当伊党副主席拿督斯里端依布拉欣和“全民共识”（MN）主席丹斯里安努亚慕沙开始大肆宣扬伊党与巫统在第16届全国大选（GE16）的“初步议席分配公式”时，选民不禁要问：他们的焦点究竟在哪里？

国阵的坚定立场： 国阵目前的优先任务与首相拿督斯里安华的施政方针高度一致——即高效治理、恢复人民经济，并拒绝在短期内举行第16届全国大选。作为团结政府中忠诚且负责任的伙伴，国阵坚决确保宏观经济的稳定不被无休止的政治内耗所干扰。

 3. 执政能力的鲜明对比：成熟稳重 vs 绝望否认

观察不同州属的政治氛围，可以发现鲜明的对比。近期有关森美兰州议会即将解散的传言被理智对待，被视为州政府的绝对主权，展现了行政上的成熟，完全没有引发任何恐慌。

反观玻璃市，情况截然不同。玻璃市州务大臣最近不得不公开强调其政权“稳固”，并极力驳斥有关不信任动议的传言。这种防御性的姿态恰恰暴露了其内部深层的焦虑。毕竟，若非事出有因，何需屡屡澄清？玻璃市的动荡局势表明，建立在情绪化基础上的政权本质上是非常脆弱的。

结语

马来西亚的选民，特别是柔佛州的选民，眼睛是雪亮的。他们不需要一个每天都在忙于应对不信任动议的州政府，也不需要一个因对未来失去信心而导致核心领袖相继“跳船”的政党。

国阵提供了反对党所无法给予的资产：确定性、稳定性和经济繁荣。选择权掌握在选民手中，国阵已做好准备，为马来西亚走向更辉煌的未来奉献最佳的服务。

Keeping options flexible for Pakatan Harapan (PH) moving ahead

The Barisan Nasional (BN) won 40 out of 56 state seats (71%) to win the Johor elections with more than 2/3rds of total seats. While I was mistaken in my earlier statement issued on the 10th of March stating that there was no clear front runner, I was right that there were many seats that were too close to call.  BN’s dominant performance in terms of the number of seats it won hides the reality that it won less than 45% of total votes (from 37.9% in GE14 to 43.2% in PRN 2022 or a 5.3% increase) which means that the combined opposition vote was more than 55% of total votes. In fact, the combined vote of PH (including MUDA) and Perikatan Nasional (PN) of approximately 750k outnumbered BN’s votes of approximately 600k by 150k. (Table 1 below)

Unfortunately, unlike GE14 where the inclusion of PAS in a multi-corner fight probably helped PH win a few marginal seats in Johor, the presence of a much stronger BERSATU together with PAS in Muhyiddin’s home state helped draw a significant proportion of Malay votes away from PH but not by enough to allow PN to win more seats despite it picking up 24.2% of the popular vote. In the end, it was the BN who benefitted this time from the multi-corner fights.

To put this into proper perspective, out of the 40 seats that were won by the BN, 20 or half were won with less than 50% of the popular vote!

What do the latest election results in Johor mean for the opposition, especially PH, which is still the largest and most influential opposition coalition? My proposal is for PH to adopt a flexible approach moving ahead in the following three areas – flexibility in our negotiation strategies with other opposition parties and coalitions at the state and federal levels, flexibility in our campaign strategies and flexibility in our timeline for GE15.

Flexibility in our negotiation strategies with other opposition parties

In light of the vote splitting among the various opposition parties and coalitions which allowed the BN to win a disproportionate % of seats in Melaka and Johor, there is obviously a need for the opposition parties to sit down and discuss various pacts and formulations for GE15. There is little point of “killing each other” on the electoral battlefield to prove who is the strongest opposition party only to end up making BN stronger than it actually is. But getting the opposition parties to sit down to talk to one another is not so straightforward because of the mutual distrust and dislike which currently exists whether it is from a party to party (PAS vs DAP, BERSATU versus PKR) or person to person (Tun M versus Anwar, Azmin’s faction in BERSATU versus the PKR leadership, Shafie Apdal versus Anwar, Hadi versus Guan Eng, just to name a few) standpoint. This is why a flexible approach has to be adopted by PH, as the largest opposition block. Discussions may take place on an informal basis on some form of electoral pact perhaps starting at the state levels to avoid 3 corner fights in seats with opposition incumbents. PH may, for example, promise not to field any candidates in the Pagoh and Mersing parliamentary seats (both BERSATU seats) and PN in return will agree not to field any candidates in Johor Bahru, Pulai and Iskandar Puteri (all PH seats). After PEJUANG’s disastrous showing in Johor where all of their candidates lost their deposits, it may make sense for this party to focus its efforts in Kedah and some of the other northern / eastern states where it has better grassroot support. WARISAN too may want to rethink its strategy of contesting in Peninsular Malaysia and put its focus back on Sabah.

Some multi-corner fights will probably be inevitable, but the basic idea here is to minimize the number of contests with opposition MPs as incumbents, whether they are from PN or PH.

In a way, PH was already adopting a flexible approach in part of this negotiation strategy. PH agreed that PKR would use its own logo / flag while DAP and AMANAH would campaign using the Harapan logo. PH also negotiated to give way to MUDA to contest in 6 state seats. Unfortunately, negotiations could not prevent MUDA and PKR from going against each other in N44 Larkin which was eventually won by the BN with 42% of the popular vote. Despite MUDA’s decision on contest in Larkin, this did not prevent PH from working together and campaigning with MUDA in some key seats including N5 Tenang, N50 Bukit Permai and N41 Puteri Wangsa (which was won by MUDA with 45% of the popular vote).

The same flexible approach should be taken in the approach towards GE15 but on a much larger stage involving much more complicated arrangements at the state and federal levels.

Flexibility in our campaign strategies

PH largely depended on large scale ‘ceramahs’ and the anti-1MDB, anti-Najib, anti-GST platforms to win GE14. We cannot depend on the same strategy if we want to have any chance to pull off a surprise win in GE15. We have to be able to employ strategies to win even in relatively low turnout and small ceramah crowd settings. This means beefing up our ground operations to do outreach to smaller groups of voters including resident associations, petty traders and hawkers, business chambers and SME associations and sports clubs, just to name a few. The personal touch of each individual candidate must be felt among different voter groups. The track record of each candidate, especially incumbents, should be highlighted in an impactful manner including via social media and personal narratives from people who have been helped by the candidate. The positive record of the PH state governments in Penang, Selangor and Negeri Sembilan needs to be highlighted to voters in other states.

More effective and creative ways of campaigning via social media including through viral videos of candidates explaining and showing their track record and aspirations to different groups of voters. Election promises or offerings to voters must be presented in more compelling and concrete ways that goes beyond a powerpoint presentation. 

At the same time, the more traditional campaign model of having ceramahs should continue, especially if we anticipate COVID related restrictions to be lifted after the 1st of April 2022. Mobilisation for great turnout especially among outstation voters and first-time voters must be done via different channels including personal appeals by family members.

Again, PH was already doing some of this in the Johor state elections but as the election results clearly show, more needs to be done.

Flexibility in our timeline for GE15

Finally, PH needs to be flexible in our timeline in anticipation of GE15. It is likely that with the strong performance in Johor, BN / UMNO will be pushing for a dissolution of parliament and a General Elections soon after the Hari Raya celebrations in May 2022. GE15 may come as soon as June 2022. We need to prepare for a June GE15 by starting the negotiations with other opposition parties / coalitions and doing the necessary groundwork now.

But at the same time, we should also be pursuing other options including extending the MOU (MOU 2.0) with Ismail Sabri’s government to beyond July 2022 as was suggested by Anthony Loke recently. This will give more time for the economy to recover and to fully open up as we move into the endemic phase of the COVID economy after the 1st of April 2022.

Being flexible does not mean we don’t have a concrete plan

Some of our supporters may not agree with my proposed approach in that it is lacking a clear direction moving forward. But the reality of politics post GE14 and post Sheraton move is that each party and coalition must be open to explore different options and configurations. In a political and economic environment that is as complex as what the country and the world is facing today, we as political leaders must do the hard work of thinking and acting strategically and then explain our actions to our supporters and to the larger public. We must avoid resorting to knee-jerk reactions and responding to immediate populist sentiment that may go against longer term interests of the opposition and also the country as a whole. For example, if PH had signed some sort of MOU with Muhyiddin last year to keep him as Prime Minister until 2023, UMNO may not have instigated the state elections in Melaka and Johor. We would definitely not have an UMNO Prime Minister who is too weak to stand up to Zahid Hamidi, his President, and Najib Razak, his former President.

Being flexible in our approach does not mean we do not have any concrete plans. On the contrary, it means that we have to have multiple concrete plans for different scenarios that may take place. Many PH leaders have criticised the post Sheraton move governments under Muhyiddin and Ismail Sabri for repeating the same policies of COVID related lockdowns but expecting different results. We should take note of our own criticism and realize that if we carry out the same strategies as before, we would be guilty of taking the same path of repeating the same moves and expecting different electoral outcomes.

Umno Denies Bribing Ex-Bersatu Reps To Defect

Umno did not offer any gifts or rewards to the two Johor Bersatu state assemblypersons who left the party, said party secretary-general Ahmad Maslan.

Ahmad, who is also Pontian MP, said that so far they had yet to receive any applications from the two individuals to join Umno.

"No gifts were promised, they quit Bersatu voluntarily and with a clear conscience, without us promising them anything… it was of their own free will.

"However, we thank them for their support for Menteri Besar (Hasni Mohammad) and BN,” he told reporters after attending a meeting with the Malaysia Makkal Sakti Party in Johor Bahru today that was also attended by Makkal Sakti president RS Thanenthiran.

Ahmad said this when asked if the two former Bersatu assemblypersons had applied to join Umno after announcing their resignation from the party.

On Thursday (Jan 27), former Puteri Wangsa assemblyperson Mazlan Bujang, who was also the state education, information, heritage and culture committee chairperson, announced his resignation as the party's Tebrau division chief and quit the party with immediate effect.

Yesterday, former Larkin assemblyperson Mohd Izhar Ahmad, who is also state investment, entrepreneur development, cooperatives and human resources committee chairperson, announced that he had quit the party with immediate effect.

Commenting on PAS and Bersatu contesting in the coming Johor state election as Perikatan Nasional (PN), Ahmad said he wasn't surprised as it was expected.

"Seems like they are repeating what happened in Malacca, so in the political dynamics, we are surely ready for any eventualities. Prior to this, we did not say that the Muafakat Nasional cooperation was final, but yesterday when PAS joined Bersatu in PN, I don't see any space (for collaboration).

"Whatever it is, we must continue to work hard and not be overconfident,” he said.

Yesterday, PN chairperson Muhyiddin Yassin, after the Muzakarah PAS Bersatu 2022, said that PAS and Bersatu would contest in the Johor polls under PN and all component parties would also use the coalition's logo in the election.

In Johor, out of the 29 percent new voters, only seven percent were aged 18-20, the remaining 22 percent were products of automatic voter registration. Perhaps the opposition parties should look back at the pre-1990 era. For three elections from 1978 to 1986, BN in Peninsular Malaysia was sandwiched by PAS on the Malay front and DAP on the non-Malay front.
 
Then, BN faced primarily PAS in Malay heartlands and DAP in Chinese constituencies. Multiethnic constituencies often saw multi-cornered fights with both PAS and DAP taking on BN, not out of enmity but as a tacit pact.

Like it or not, the peninsula politics has reverted to the 1980s, with PN as the expansion of PAS with another Umno splinter partner in Bersatu; and Harapan as the expanded partnership of DAP with three direct and indirect Umno splinters: PKR, Amanah and Muda.

Ibrahim Ali: True Umno A 'Lame Duck', But PAS Is 'Mentally Sick'

Parti Bumiputera Perkasa Malaysia (Putra) president Ibrahim Ali today ridiculed PAS, whose president recently criticised Umno for abandoning their friendship after Umno was "saved" and "healed" by the Islamist party.

While Ibrahim (above) said he agreed with PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang for saying that Umno was a "lame duck", he claimed that PAS was no better than Umno for itself has changed allies many times, including with those whom PAS had regarded as kafir (infidels).

"It is true that Umno broke its leg. A broken leg can be healed by the traditional way of bone setting massages, or in this time of science and technology, one can even make a prosthetic leg to be able to walk. 

"If one really follows the treatment and abide by the advice of the doctor, there is a chance that the leg can be nursed back to health.

"On the other hand, PAS is mentally sick. The easiest example to show this was when PAS said that it was haram for voters to choose non-Muslims as their leaders, but later they said it is permissible.

"PAS used to accuse DAP as evil. Later it accused Umno as more evil than DAP. When PAS became friends with DAP in Pakatan Rakyat, Hadi could hug with Lim Kit Siang and Lim Guan Eng, and he criticised Umno.

"But then, PAS came together with Umno in Muafakat Nasional. Later it abandoned Muafakat and joined Perikatan Nasional. Isn't this confusing? Weird but true. Isn't this a sign of mental illness?" Ibrahim said in his statement.

On Friday, Hadi reportedly accused Umno of being ungrateful following the latter's reluctance to forge an electoral pact. 

The PAS chief branded Umno as "a lame duck", which was saved by PAS but now wanted to swim on its own after it was healed.

PAS has not abandoned its Muafakat pact with Umno, but the two parties have been at odds especially since PAS chose to join Bersatu in PN.

Frictions between PAS and Umno have been increasingly apparent since the Malacca election last November, which saw both parties on different corners. 

Eventually, Umno triumphed and PAS was vanquished.

MEMAHAMI POLITIK UMNO

"Government is not a team. It is a loose confederation of warring tribes." - Sir Humphrey Appleby 

Tadi masa makan malam bersama abah dan mak aku, abah aku bertanya satu soalan simple tentang politik. Memandangkan dalam keluarga aku ni, aku yang paling cakna pasal politik, jadi selalunya bila isu-isu politik berlaku ni abah aku akan tanya pada aku.

Soalan dia ialah, "kenapa Hishamuddin (Hussein Onn) tu?", soalan dia memang kurang jelas, tapi aku faham, soalan abah aku ialah "betul ke Hishamuddin Hussein nak jadi Presiden UMNO?"

Jawapan pendek dan ringkas (sebab aku tak nak bosankan mak ayah aku dengan sembang politik), ialah "dia nak jadi Presiden UMNO, tapi dia pro-PN. Akar umbi tak suka dia. Dia tu Pengerusi UMNO Sembrong, sebelah je dengan Kluang. UMNO Kluang pun tak suka dia, macam mana dia nak jadi Presiden?"

Tapi ini jawapan panjang aku. 

Ramai orang laymen melihat UMNO ni sebagai satu parti and that's it. Kesilapan ini sering dilakukan oleh cybertrooper PH yang menganggap bahawa UMNO ni ialah sebuah parti semata-mata. Kalau anggap macam tu, alamatnya memang korang tak faham lagi bagaimana politik Melayu berfungsi.

Politik Melayu - seperti politik-politik negara Asia yang lain, adalah politik kabilah. Politik kabilah tidak ada ideologi atau falsafah. Politik kabilah adalah politik yang berbeza daripada politik Eropah dan Amerika.

Kerana politik Asia tidak mengalami Rennaisance dan Reformation. Politik Asia tidak ada sosok Thomas Aquinas, Martin Luther, Jean Jacques Rosseau, Voltaire, John Locke, Thomas Hobbes atau Karl Marx. Politik Asia dan Afrika cuma ada tiga peringkat sahaja, sebelum imperialisme, semasa imperialisme, selepas imperialisme.

Seringkas-ringkas politik Asia ini juga ramai yang keliru sebab ia mempunyai jaringan yang kompleks. Ia ringkas kerana tidak mempunyai falsafah, tapi ia kompleks sebab setiap keputusan politik yang dilakukan oleh pemimpin adalah kerana keputusan kabilah.

Dan UMNO bukanlah sebuah parti - tapi sebuah pertubuhan yang disertai oleh pelbagai ketua kabilah. Sebab tu la kau tengok dalam persidangan UMNO tu, muka-muka yang pergi semuanya sama ada ketua dalam kampung, dalam taman, yang ada konco-konco mereka dalam organisasi.

Dan konco mereka ni pun ada berlawan dengan konco yang lain dalam merebut kuasa.

Jadi kalau kau cakap UMNO ni sebuah parti, kau cuma nampak politik Malaysia ni satu layer sahaja.

Daripada kabilah-kabilah kecil ni, mereka bernaung dengan kabilah yang lebih besar dan paling besar ialah kabilah macam Mahathir, Anwar, Najib, Muhyiddin, Hadi Awang dan lain-lain.

Ya, aku letakkan Hadi Awang sekali dalam UMNO sebab PAS ni asalnya dari UMNO, yang berpisah dari UMNO sejak 1951. DNA yang sama walaupun mengalami mutasi sekitar tahun 70an selepas krisis politik di Kelantan pada tahun 1977. (zaman Asri Muda)

Anwar sudah semestinya dari DNA UMNO, begitu juga Mahathir dan Muhyiddin Yassin walaupun pakai lambang lain selain dacing.

Kalau kau perasan, banyak bekas pemimpin UMNO (kecuali Tun Razak dan Tun Abdullah Badawi, Najib belum boleh dianggap bekas sebab masih aktif), semua keluar UMNO, dan sama ada tubuh parti baru, atau join parti lain.

Onn Jaafar keluar UMNO pada tahun 1951 selepas ditolak oleh akar umbi bila dia nak masukkan orang bukan Melayu dalam UMNO.

Tunku Abdul Rahman dan Tun Hussein Onn keluar UMNO pada krisis UMNO 1988, dan menyokong Tengku Razaleigh sebelum meninggal dunia.

Tun Mahathir dia punya rekod keluar masuk UMNO dah macam pintu 7-Eleven. Bunyi "teng-neng" tu orang dah tak heran lagi dah. Dia tubuhkan Parti Pertubuhan Peribumi Bersatu Malaysia (PPBM), yang kalau kau translate ke English, bunyinya UMNO juga lebih kurang. Kemudian tubuh parti Pejuang. Muhyiddin Yassin pun pernah jadi Timbalan Presiden UMNO. 

Anwar Ibrahim dipecat dari UMNO, dan menubuhkan PKR, tapi asalnya dari UMNO juga.

Senang cerita, kalau kau bukan dari UMNO, kau takkan berkuasa. Sebab it has designed that way since the beginning. UMNO ditubuhkan di Istana Johor pada tahun 1946, maknanya hubungan UMNO dan istana tu macam simbiosis.

Apabila krisis perlembagaan antara kerajaan dan istana berlaku pada lewat 80an dan awal 90an, ia menjadi krisis walaupun Barisan Nasional pegang 2/3 majoriti dalam kerusi Parlimen.

Dalam clash of power antara Mahathir selaku Presiden UMNO dengan istana, ia mencetuskan krisis sebab dua idea bercanggah. Idea Mahathir ialah dia adalah Presiden UMNO, parti terbesar dalam Barisan Nasional, yang dipilih oleh rakyat, maka Mahathir mewakili idea "vox populae vox dei" atau suara rakyat suara keramat.

Now, soal adakah Mahathir ni bawak suara rakyat ni betul ke tak, tu kita boleh pertikaikan (senang cerita krisis awal 90s tu dia menunggang rakyat la, lepas krisis kayu hoki dan golf, aku malas nak ulas lebih), tapi prinsipal Mahathir ialah dia dipilih rakyat dan istana cuma dapat kuasa melalui keturunan.

Tetapi ramai yang tak aware bahawa parti UMNO ni ditubuhkan oleh istana. Dan, kalau kita faham politik Melayu sebelum imperialisme - para hulubalang berebut-rebut mahu dapatkan kepercayaan sultan.

Media Statement by Dr. Ong Kian Ming, Member of Parliament for Bangi on the 24th of April, 2020

UMNO’s dilemma in the Perikatan Nasional (PN) coalition government – Part 1

It has been more than one month since Muhyiddin Yassin’s Perikatan National (PN) cabinet was sworn in on the 10th of March 2020. Each political party within this uneasy coalition faces their unique political challenges in operating as part of the government. But no party faces bigger questions and challenges than UMNO as it grapples with the question of how it wants to work with BERSATU. This is UMNO’s biggest dilemma within the PN government.

From the outset, let me be clear on this point - UMNO leaders and members would much prefer to be in government together with BERSATU than to be in the opposition. In government, UMNO would have access to the privileges of power including access to positions in Ministries, Government Agencies and GLCs. But there is NOTHING about the arrangement in the current PN government which UMNO would find acceptable in the longer term. Most importantly, from a political strategy perspective, UMNO leaders must realize that BERSATU’s ultimate goal is to replace UMNO in the political arena as the dominant Malay party in government. This is the only way that BERSATU can survive post GE15 and UMNO knows this.

After ruling the country for over 60 years, UMNO is not used to playing the role of No.2 in government. And yet, this is the position they find themselves in today. With 41 elected Members of Parliament (MPs), they have more MPs than BERSATU, who only have 29 MPs (this includes the 10 MPs from PKR but does not include the 5 MPs who are supporting Tun Mahathir). And yet, BERSATU have more Ministers (11 including the Prime Minister versus 9 for UMNO) and Deputy Ministers (15 versus 8 for UMNO) than UMNO. Most of the key Ministries are also being helmed by BERSATU MPs (Education, Home Affairs, Economy, Rural Development, Trade and Industry) or individuals aligned to the Prime Minister (Finance) with UMNO having perhaps only one relatively ‘senior’ ministry, namely Defence. Two out of the Four Senior Ministers are also from BERSATU with UMNO having only one Senior Minister. 

UMNO is also facing the unprecedented experience of its President, Deputy President and two of its Vice Presidents (VP) not having any government positions. Ismail Sabri, the Minister for Defence and one of the four Senior Ministers is the only UMNO VP in the cabinet. Furthermore, UMNO MPs who are elected members of the UMNO Supreme Council were not given any government positions  while UMNO MPs who are not part of the top leadership of the party were made Ministers. UMNO Sabah was also completely left out of the cabinet in favour of BERSATU MPs who had left UMNO and PKR. 

This situation is not one which must sit comfortably with UMNO’s leadership. This is why the statement that was issued by the UMNO president on the 12th of March 2020, after an UMNO Supreme Council meeting, put so many caveats in its support for Muhyiddin Yassin’s government. There was no mention of any efforts to strengthen Perikatan Nasional (PN) as a ruling coalition. Instead, the UMNO president went out of his way to mention efforts to strengthen its partnership with PAS via Muafakat Nasional (MN) and to build up the strength of Barisan Nasional (BN). Most importantly, the statement ended with a commitment to support the new government only until the next general election (GE15).

Any form of cooperation between BERSATU and UMNO will likely cease once parliament is dissolved, whenever this happens. It is hard to see how UMNO and BERSATU can agree to any seat allocation formula. UMNO and PAS will have their hands full in allocating the 100 parliament seats in Peninsular Malaysia where both parties contested in GE14 under a Muafakat Nasional (MN) formula in GE15. UMNO, PAS and BERSATU competed in 47 parliament seats in Peninsular Malaysia in GE14. These include seats like Titiwangsa (where BERSATU’s Rina Harun, the current Minister of Women, Family and Community Development defeated Johari Abdul Ghani, former Minister of Finance II and who is still the chair of UMNO in the Federal Territories) and Ketereh (where current Federal Territories Minister, Annuar Musa from UMNO defeated current Education Minister, Mohd Radzi bin Jidin from BERSATU who was subsequently appointed a Senator). 

The 47 parliament seats also includes seats which feature UMNO MPs who subsequently joined BERSATU post GE14 such as Jeli (Mustapha Mohamed, currently a Minister in the Prime Minister’s Office), Larut (Hamzah bin Zainuddin, current Home Minister), Mersing (Abdul Latiff bin Ahmad, current Minister of Rural Development) and Masjid Tanah (Mas Ermieyati binti Samsudin, the current Deputy Minister of Tourism). It is hard to imagine UMNO having many positive feelings about these defectors much less negotiating with BERSATU to allow these incumbent BERSATU MPs to continue to contest in these seats with UMNO and PAS’ support. 

In addition, the current cabinet also features former PKR MPs who joined BERSATU and whose seats were contested by both UMNO and PAS in GE14 including Gombak (Azmin Ali), Indera Mahkota (Saifuddin Abdullah), Bandar Tun Razak (Kamaruddin Jaafar), Batu Pahat (Mohd Rashid bin Hasnon) and Nibong Tebal (Mansor bin Othman). Again, it is hard to see UMNO or PAS both giving way to these BERSATU MPs in GE15. 

UMNO has shown that it can defeat BERSATU even while it was in opposition at the state and federal levels in the Tanjung Piai and Kimanis parliamentary by-elections in Johor and Sabah respectively. With its grassroots support intact and with the continued nurturing of its relationship with PAS, there is no need for UMNO (and PAS) to make concessions or to work with BERSATU in GE15.

Knowing this, what is BERSATU’s likely response in the short term (over the next year) and closer to GE15? And what is UMNO’s likely strategy? This will be covered in Part 2.

How the Perak MB Crisis Unfolded

The latest Perak menteri besar ouster marks the third time the state government has fallen since its constitutional crisis in 2009.

The first was triggered when three Pakatan Rakyat assemblymen defected, causing the collapse of the state administration under then menteri besar Datuk Seri Nizar Jamaluddin of PAS.

The second time occurred earlier this year as a result of the collapse of the Pakatan Harapan (PH) federal administration when Langkawi MP Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad tendered his resignation as prime minister.

Lawmakers from Bersatu, a party Dr Mahathir founded, left PH en masse, including Prime Minister Tan Sri Muhyiddin Yassin and former Perak menteri besar Datuk Seri Ahmad Faizal Azumu.

Dubbed the “Sheraton Move”, this led to the formation of the Perikatan Nasional (PN) federal government.

PH’s fall in Putrajaya triggered a cascade of states ending up in the hands of PN – Perak, Kedah and Johor, among others.

Below is a timeline of how Faizal’s administration fell in just a few weeks:

October 29 – Faizal had said he did not believe claims that Perak Umno has been conspiring with opposition parties to overthrow the PN state government.

He had said he had full trust in Perak Umno state liaison chairman Datuk Saarani Mohamad, whom he considers a political mentor. 

Earlier, Saarani also denied allegations that Perak Umno was conspiring with opposition parties in the state to seize the menteri besar post.

November 18 – Umno’s Pengkalan Baharu assemblyman Datuk Abdul Manaf Hashim filed a motion of confidence through a letter to state Speaker Datuk Mohamad Zahir Abdul Khalid.

December 4 – At 8.30am, Umno’s Temenggor assemblyman Salbiah Mohamed and DAP’s Pasir Pinji assemblyman Howard Lee both filed emergency motions for the confidence vote.

The vote was accepted by Zahir, who acknowledged that it was a matter of urgent public interest.

In his speech on his motion, Manaf had told the state House that, due to the Covid-19 pandemic, it would be unwise to call for a dissolution of the assembly and a state election to determine Faizal’s legitimacy.

Manaf was supported by PAS state commissioner and Gunong Semanggol assemblyman Razman Zakaria, who said a change of government in the current situation was tantamount to a betrayal of public trust.

When invited to put in their two cents, the state opposition said it will not participate in the debate on the motion.

This led to the speaker calling for a vote and a division of the assembly form of voting was requested.

All assemblyman then cast their votes on a sheet of paper before passing it to the assembly’s heralds (bentara), who carried boxes to collect their ballots.

Zahir then announced that Faizal had lost the confidence vote, with 48 votes against him and only 10 in support. One vote was considered spoilt or abstained.
 
At 4.30pm, Perak Secretary Datuk Ahmad Suaidi Abdul Rahim and Perak Legal Adviser Datuk Rohana Abdul Malek were summoned for an audience with state ruler Sultan Nazrin Shah at Istana Kinta in Ipoh.

At 5pm, Zahir was called in for an audience with the sultan on what had happened that morning.

Faizal was also granted an audience with the sultan after Zahir left.

After his audience, Faizal told the press that he was Perak’s caretaker menteri besar.

December 5 – At 9am, during a cheque-giving ceremony, Faizal told reporters that he would resign as menteri besar after his successor has been appointed.

At 11am, Sultan Nazrin granted an audience to three state PH leaders – DAP’s Nga Kor Ming, PKR’s Farhash Wafa Salvador Rizal Mubarak and Amanah’s Datuk Asmuni Awi.

At 11.30am, Perak Umno liaison chairman and MB frontrunner Datuk Saarani Mohamad was granted an audience with the sultan.

After Saarani left the palace, Dewan Negara member Datuk Seri Mohd Annuar Zaini told the press that the party leaders had informed the sultan of their positions. However, no menteri besar candidates were mentioned.

At 3pm, Faizal was seen entering the palace for a brief audience with the sultan. Faizal then tendered his resignation as menteri besar. The move automatically dissolved the state executive committee and the PN state administration.

At 6pm, Faizal announced his resignation at Laman Seri Perak, the old menteri besar residence.

However, his parting words “Jemput datang ke Sri Satria nanti” had tongues wagging on whether he is gunning for the deputy prime minister post.

Meanwhile, Perak PAS commissioner Razman Zakaria said he will not take sides during this crisis, and support both Bersatu and Umno.

He also said the state chapter’s mandate is to defend the current government and any decision on a new one will be up to the party’s central leadership.

Later, PAS deputy president Datuk Seri Tuan Ibrahim Tuan Man was reported as saying that the Islamist party will meet to discuss its cooperation with Umno in Muafakat Nasional and PN.

At 8.12pm, Umno president Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi arrived at the party’s state headquarters to attend a special state-level meeting, where is was expected to discuss menteri besar candidates.

The 9pm meeting chaired by Saarani was also attended by former Supreme Council member and Padang Rengas MP Datuk Seri Nazri Aziz, Perak Umno deputy chairman Datuk Azian Osman and other state leaders.

After waiting nearly two hours outside the Umno building in Ipoh, many leaders remained tight-lipped over the night’s agenda.

Meanwhile, Saarani gave the press the slip.

Today, Zahid is scheduled to meet Sultan Nazrin at Istana Kinta at 10am to discuss the menteri besar crisis.

Don’t fret over MN, just pick PAS or Umno, says Khairuddin

Malay-Muslim voters, especially PAS and Umno supporters, need not scratch their heads over the status of Muafakat National, the political bloc forged between the two parties, a former PAS leader said.

Khairuddin Aman Razali said Malay-Muslim voters should either support PAS or Umno in the coming 15th general election to avoid any further split between the two largest Malay-based parties.

The parties formed MN in September 2019 as an electoral pact aimed at uniting the ummah.

However, relations between them have grown increasingly strained after PAS joined Bersatu to form Perikatan Nasional when Bersatu president Muhyiddin Yassin was the prime minister.

In May, Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi had even said MN was “as good as dead”.

But Khairuddin, the Kuala Nerus MP who quit PAS in March, said it was normal for certain leaders to attack each other although there were those who wanted the two parties to remain united.

“So, there is no need to conclude that MN is buried, as no Umno or PAS leader has come out to declare it so. As long as there are those who want MN, it would not be buried,” he said.

Khairuddin said this when asked to comment on Zahid’s riposte to PAS president Abdul Hadi Awang’s statement that there were those who wanted GE15 to be held as soon as possible as they were “power crazy”.

Zahid, who is among the Umno leaders pushing for an early election, responded by saying that Hadi was afraid of losing many seats if the nationwide polls were held earlier.

Khairuddin said that even though he wanted PAS and Umno to continue working together under MN, it did not mean Bersatu should be left out of the pact.

“We understand that Umno does not want anything to do with Bersatu,” the former PAS central committee member said, referring to Umno’s decision to cut ties with Muhyiddin’s party.

“So PAS must play the peacemaker.”

He said no good would come from PAS abandoning Umno and working with PN, as proven when PN lost in the Johor and Melaka state elections.

“In my opinion, it would be a loss (for PAS) to leave Umno and work with Bersatu, but that is the president’s and the party’s right (on who they choose to work with).”

He said although Hadi’s strategy had backfired by choosing PN over Umno in the Johor and Melaka elections, he did not discount the possibility that teaming up with Umno as well would have reaped benefits at that time.
